bib.title: EvoPrompting: Language Models for Code-Level Neural Architecture Search

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "EvoPrompting: Language Models for Code-Level Neural Architecture Search", Angelica Chen (NYU), David M. Dohan (OpenAI), David R. So (Jane Street); work done at Google DeepMind. NeurIPS 2023 (37th Conference), arXiv:2302.14838v3, 16 Nov 2023.

COVERAGE: 87,800 of 87,800 chars extracted. I read the body in full (chars 0-~11k of references excluded), the appendix A.1, A.3-A.4 captions, A.6 (Table 3) and A.7-A.8 in full. I skimmed the references (~46k-55k). I skipped the seed and discovered model source listings in A.2, A.4 and A.5 (about 58.9k-77.8k) as code. Figures were not rendered. I used the captions in the extraction only.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Loop design: an LM acts as the crossover and mutation operator in an evolutionary NAS loop. Each round it generates candidates from few-shot prompts built from the top survivors, the candidates are trained and scored, the top p become parents, and all other evaluated children prompt-tune the LM (soft prompt) for the next round.
  number: none
  setup: Algorithm 1; p=10 parents, k=2 in-context examples, T=10 rounds, m=10 prompts, n=16 samples per prompt (Appx A.1).
  quote: "the combination of evolutionary prompt engineering with soft prompt-tuning, a method we term EVOPROMPTING, consistently finds diverse and high performing models."
  where: abstract; Alg. 1-3, pp. 5-6

- Headline result: on CLRS, discovered GNNs beat the Triplet-GMPNN SOTA on 21 of 30 tasks at similar model size. My count of Table 3 agrees: the baseline is best on 9 tasks.
  number: 21/30
  setup: searched on 3 tasks only (articulation points, Graham scan, Kruskal). The best discovered models were then evaluated on all 30. 62B PaLM, 1600 models per search. The search covers only the triplet representation, with 9 seeds.
  quote: "EVOPROMPTING is able to design novel architectures that outperform current state-of-the-art models on 21 out of 30 algorithmic reasoning tasks while maintaining similar model size."
  where: abstract; Table 3, p. 27

- Ablations on MNIST-1D: removing any component hurts. Naive few-shot prompting is unsuccessful. Random parents plus prompt-tuning is no better than naive prompting. Fit parents without prompt-tuning is much worse than the full method.
  number: none (read from Fig. 2a/2b, no numeric table)
  setup: MNIST-1D, 4 seeds (GRU, CNN, MLP, larger CNN), top 20 models per variant, 1600 samples each.
  quote: "Interestingly, Figure 2a indicates that prompting with randomly selected parents combined with prompt-tuning is no more effective than naive prompting alone."
  where: p. 8

- Selection matters for sample efficiency: the random-parents baseline plateaus after about 200 individuals, while the other variants plateau much later. The full method plateaus highest.
  number: ~200 individuals
  setup: MNIST-1D, max fitness vs number of children generated, 100 bootstrap samples of size 20.
  quote: "The random parents baseline plateaus the quickest, reaching a maximum fitness by the time approximately 200 individuals have been generated."
  where: p. 8

- Heapsort example (CONCATREP): +125% OOD accuracy for +6.68% model size.
  number: 125.19%, 6.68%
  setup: CLRS heapsort OOD accuracy, 69.9 vs 31.0 from Ibarz et al. Table 3 also lists 19.45 for the authors' own baseline reimplementation, so the gain is smaller against it.
  quote: "on the heapsort algorithm CONCAT REP increased OOD accuracy by 125.19% while only increasing model size by 6.68% over the baseline."
  where: p. 10

- Table 1 gains versus the Ibarz et al. baseline:
  Bubble Sort 88.9±2.8% vs 67.7±5.5%.
  DFS 68.1±1.4% vs 47.8±4.2%.
  Quicksort 85.2±4.3% vs 64.6±5.1%.
  Articulation Points 93.5±1.8% vs 88.3±2.0%.
  Several gains come with smaller models.
  number: as listed
  setup: the best of 5 selected discovered models per task, baseline numbers from the paper.
  quote: "Bubble Sort C ONCAT REP 568533 524477 88.9 ± 2.8% 67.7± 5.5%"
  where: Table 1, p. 9

- Fitness is the negative product of validation error and model size, with an error cap to stop the search gaming it through tiny models. The prompt conditions on target metrics.
  number: target size = 90% of the minimum parent size; target accuracy = 102% of the maximum parent accuracy
  setup: all experiments.
  quote: "We set the target model size as 90% of the minimum model size of the parent models, rounded to the nearest 100 parameters, and the target validation accuracy as 102% of the maximum validation accuracy of the parent models"
  where: pp. 5-6
  also: "we use the negative product of the validation error and the model size as the fitness"

- Selected parents are removed from the population and cannot be reused. Only non-selected children train the soft prompt.
  quote: "Once these models have been selected, they are permanently removed from the population and cannot be used again as parents for crossover."
  where: p. 6

- Infrastructure: 62B PaLM, code-fine-tuned. Mixed temperature sampling gives diversity. Between rounds it is prompt-tuned (Lester et al., 2021) for 5 epochs.
  number: 62B; temperatures [0.2, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0]; soft prompt length 16, batch 16, lr 0.1; 160 models per round, 1600 total
  quote: "yielding a total of 160 models generated per round and 1600 models generated during the entire search."
  where: p. 7

- NATS-Bench (Appx A.7) is competitive but not clearly better than the other NAS methods.
  number: CIFAR-10 test 93.11±0.90 vs REA 93.22±0.16; ImageNet-16-120 test 45.15±0.51 vs REA 45.94±0.92
  setup: size search space. Other methods' numbers are from Dong et al. 2021. The LM is handicapped because it emits "64:64:64:64:64" strings.
  quote: "EVOPROMPT - ING 90.38± 0.33 93.11± 0.90 70.47± 0.23 70.39± 0.58 45.32± 0.26 45.15± 0.51"
  where: Table 4, p. 29

- Round-over-round gains are not monotone on both axes: test error improves while size trades off in rounds 0-2 and 6-10, and both improve in rounds 3-5.
  quote: "In rounds 0-2 and 6-10, EVOPROMPTING improves test error while trading off model size."
  where: p. 8

LIMITS
- The authors concede there is no extensive comparison against standard NAS: "our study is limited by the lack of an extensive comparison against other standard NAS techniques" (p. 10).
- Figure 3 shows more variance on CLRS than on MNIST-1D.
- The ablations are shown only as Pareto and fitness curves, with no table and no seeds count. The "bootstrap of 20" is not independent runs.
- The search is run on 3 CLRS tasks. The "21 of 30" is transfer of 5 hand-picked discovered models, so the best of 5 per task is taken. The best-per-task selection and the 2000-step training budget may favour the winners.
- Table 3 shows that against the authors' own baseline reimplementation some gains shrink. The OOD numbers are not all significant, since several differences are within one std.
- Search space is narrow on CLRS (triplet representation only).
- The cost in compute is not given: one P100 per child, 1600 children per search, plus 62B PaLM inference and prompt-tuning.
- The generality claim to non-NAS tasks is untested ("We leave the adaptation ... to future work"). The method dates to PaLM-62B and 2023.

BUILDS ON
Real et al. 2017/2018 (evolutionary NAS); So et al. 2019/2021; Lester et al. 2021 (prompt-tuning); Brown et al. 2020 (few-shot prompting); Lehman et al. 2022 (LM as mutation operator, Sodarace); Meyerson et al. 2023 (concurrent, LM crossover with MAP-Elites); Dohan et al. 2022 (prompts as parameters); Brooks et al. 2022 (in-context policy iteration); Greydanus 2020 (MNIST-1D); Veličković et al. 2022 (CLRS); Ibarz et al. 2022 (Triplet-GMPNN); Chowdhery et al. 2022 (PaLM); Dong et al. 2021 (NATS-Bench).

CODE
Listing 1 prompt format (p. 6), reflowed from the extraction:
"""Metrics:
{'num_params': '4800', 'val_accuracy': '0.865'}
"""
class Model(nn.Module): ...
(2-shot in practice, ending with the target metrics line and an open class Model.)
Pseudocode, Alg. 1 steps 6-11: C <- CROSSMUT(pi_theta_t, P, m, k, n); C_evaled <- FILTERANDEVAL(C, T, D, alpha); G <- G + C_evaled; P <- GETTOP(G, p); theta_{t+1} <- TRAIN(theta_t, C_evaled \ P).
FILTERANDEVAL keeps a child only if c.error < alpha, with score s <- -c.model_size x c.error.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p. 2): overview of the loop (seeds, LM candidates, train and evaluate, select top as in-context examples, all evaluated children prompt-tune the LM). Fastest explanation of the loop.
- Fig 2a/2b (p. 8): Pareto frontiers of size vs test error, and max fitness vs samples generated, for full / no prompt-tuning / random parents / naive. This is the ablation evidence.
- Fig 3 (p. 8): max fitness vs samples on 3 CLRS tasks.
- Fig 4 (p. 18): per-round average size and error. Fig 5: validation accuracy trajectories of the discovered models.
I did not render the figures.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found. The extraction is clean. Tables 3 and 4 have some wrapped lines.
- Inconsistency: the text calls α an "upper threshold" for error, but Appx Table 2 labels it "Lower threshold for test error", value 0.5.
- The text says the score uses the "negative product of validation error and model size", but the MNIST-1D Pareto plots use test error.
- Intro says "(Appendix 3)" for the 21/30 result, but it is Table 3 in A.6 (p. 27).
- Scratch text is at /tmp/papers-t3/loop-2/evoprompting/t.txt.
